title: Algerian War of Independence 1954-1962
welcome_lead: From the Aurès mountains to the Évian Accords, study the bitter struggle that ended 132 years of French rule in Algeria.
meta_desc: IBDP History Independence Movements Adventure 2: Algerian War 1954-1962 and the end of French Algeria.
final_note: You have followed the path from All Saints' Day attacks to the Évian Accords. The war's wounds remain raw in both nations.

concepts.def: Front de Libération Nationale, the leading Algerian nationalist movement founded in 1954.
All Saints' Day attacks of 1 November 1954 that launched the war.
Urban campaign in which French paratroopers under General Massu used torture to crush FLN networks.
European settlers in Algeria, around one million strong by the 1950s.
Organisation de l'Armée Secrète, settler paramilitary opposing Algerian independence.
Cease-fire and political settlement leading to Algerian independence on 5 July 1962.

walkthroughs.body_html: The FLN launched coordinated attacks on 1 November 1954, demanding independence from France. French Algeria, governed as an integral part of metropolitan France with around a million European settlers, refused to negotiate, declaring the FLN bandits and committing escalating military force.

In 1956-57 French paratroopers under Jacques Massu used systematic torture and forced disappearances to dismantle FLN cells in the Algerian capital. Successes on the ground generated political backlash in France, especially when journalists and conscripts exposed abuses. Rural regroupement camps displaced millions of Algerians.

The May 1958 crisis brought Charles de Gaulle back to power. Initially ambiguous, he eventually accepted self-determination. Negotiations at Évian in March 1962 produced a cease-fire and referendums in France and Algeria. Independence was declared on 5 July 1962. Estimates of Algerian deaths range from 300,000 to over a million.
